### The read-only interior task {#sec-arch-passive-decoder}

**With `query_independent=True` (ISLA-DTT) the prediction points are
read-only: at every slice layer they read the slices the boundary formed at
that layer and never write into them, and after it they read the boundary
cells (@sec-arch-global-read), so the prediction at a point is a function
of that point and the boundary alone.** A read-only point is encoded as an
interacting one is (its exact geometry and its own input layer `qt.seed`)
and runs through the same twelve slice layers with
the same parameters as the boundary tokens. Only its measure bias differs:
$\ell_q = -\infty$, so every softmax over tokens gives it zero weight. It
takes no part in the routing prototypes, the anchors $z_s, m_s$ (step c),
the routing weights $a_{is}$ (step f), the slice states $Z_s$ (step g) or
the head frame's anchors (stage 4). It still forms its own logits, its
relational invariants against the anchors and its read-back weights
$\pi_{qs}$, and it reads $b_q = \sum_s \pi_{qs} Z_s$ (step h). The boundary
tokens therefore compute what they compute in the surface task whatever
points are requested, and a request split into chunks, permuted, or reduced
to one point returns the same predictions to $10^{-12}$ in float64
(`test_query_independent_interior_contracts`). On AirfRANS checkpoints
trained with the compiled path after its fault was fixed (their In-flight
note is in @sec-query-population), in float32 every change of the request of
@tbl-query-population moves ISLA-DTT's error by at most
`{python} Markdown(sci(DTT_QDEV))`, float32 roundoff. ISLA-DTT has no routing-mass
parameter.

A read-only point reads at matched depth: at layer $\ell$ it reads the
slices formed from the boundary states at layer $\ell$, the depth its own
state has reached. That alignment accounts for much of the read-only model's
accuracy. @tbl-arch-read-depth isolates it on read-only points without the
boundary read: a control with the same parameters, in which every layer's
points read slices formed from the *final* boundary state, is markedly less
accurate on both interior datasets, while doubling the slice count changes
neither the read-only nor the interacting model beyond seed noise.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-arch-read-depth
#| output: asis
REPORT = (RESEARCH / "dtt" / "REPORT.md").read_text()
def md_section_table(title_prefix):
    sec = REPORT.split("\n### ")
    body = next(s for s in sec if s.startswith(title_prefix))
    rows = [l for l in body.splitlines() if l.startswith("| ") and not l.startswith("| arm") and not l.startswith("|---")]
    return {r.split("|")[1].strip(): [c.strip() for c in r.split("|")[2:-1]] for r in rows}
def triple(s):
    return [float(x) for x in s.split(" / ")]
af = md_section_table("E6 interim on AirfRANS"); car = md_section_table("E6 interim on the car")
pick = lambda t, pref: next(v for k, v in t.items() if k.startswith(pref))
ROWS = [("read-only points, matched depth (base)", "P, 512 slices (E3)", "P, 256 slices (E5)", "P"),
        ("read-only points reading the final boundary state", "FINAL control", "FINAL control", "P"),
        ("read-only points, twice the slices", "P, 1,024 slices", "P, 512 slices", "P"),
        ("interacting points (base)", "I, 512 slices", "I, 256 slices (E5)", "I"),
        ("interacting points, twice the slices", "I, 1,024 slices", "I, 512 slices", "I")]
base = {("car", "P"): triple(pick(car, "P, 512 slices (E3)")[2]), ("af", "P"): triple(pick(af, "P, 256 slices (E5)")[2]),
        ("car", "I"): triple(pick(car, "I, 512 slices")[2]), ("af", "I"): triple(pick(af, "I, 256 slices (E5)")[2])}
fmt3 = lambda v: " / ".join(f"{x:.4f}" for x in v)
out = "| model | DrivAerML Volume: p / v / nut | ÷ its base | AirfRANS: p / v / nut | ÷ its base |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n"
for lab, kc, ka, kind in ROWS:
    vc, va = triple(pick(car, kc)[2]), triple(pick(af, ka)[2])
    rc = " / ".join(f"{x / y:.2f}" for x, y in zip(vc, base[("car", kind)]))
    ra = " / ".join(f"{x / y:.2f}" for x, y in zip(va, base[("af", kind)]))
    out += f"| {lab} | {fmt3(vc)} | {rc} | {fmt3(va)} | {ra} |\n"
print(out)
print(": Matched-depth reading and slice count, without the boundary read: relative L2 of interior pressure / "
      "velocity / eddy viscosity (p / v / nut), float32, seed means of two seeds (42, 43). DrivAerML Volume task: 48 held-out "
      "cars, 200,000 boundary cells and 200,000 prediction points per car; AirfRANS interior task: 200 test airfoils, "
      "100,000 prediction points from one contiguous window of the stored points, so ratios compare like with like and the "
      "absolute errors do not carry over (@sec-interior-airfrans). Instrument: on the car, ISLA at 512 wide, 512 slices "
      "(1,024 doubled), 3.75e-4, raw slice reads; on the airfoil, ISLA at 384 wide, 256 slices (512 doubled), 5e-4, raw slice "
      "reads (@sec-study-configurations); checkpoints of the nearest-token form (@sec-checkpoint-form). How to read this: each ÷ compares a row with the base row of its own kind (read-only "
      "or interacting) on the same dataset, above one meaning less accurate; the second row changes only which boundary state "
      "the points read, the third and fifth only the slice count; the two interacting car rows were trained on code that differs "
      "beyond the slice count, so their ratio is not a clean slice-count effect. Data: research/dtt/REPORT.md, its "
      "matched-depth sections on AirfRANS and on the car.")
```

#### The global boundary read {#sec-arch-global-read}

**A read-only point also reads the boundary cells themselves: after every
slice layer each prediction point adds a measure-weighted average of the
cells' states over the whole boundary, weighted by a learned kernel of where
each cell sits relative to the point and by how well their states
match.** For a point $q$ and a cell $j$, with $\rho_{qj} \equiv r_q - r_j$,
the kernel sees the pair's invariants $\iota_{qj}$: the distance
$\lvert\rho_{qj}\rvert$, its logarithm, $\log(\lvert\rho_{qj}\rvert /
\lvert s_q\rvert)$ (the distance in units of the point's own distance to
the surface), the cosines of $\hat\rho_{qj}$ with $\hat n_j$, $\hat\nu_q$
and every $\hat g_k$, and $\hat\nu_q \cdot \hat n_j$ and $\hat n_j \cdot
\hat g_k$; each of the cell's shared vector channels $V_{ja}$ adds its
cosines with $\hat\rho_{qj}$ and $\hat\nu_q$ (`tree_pair_invariants`). One MLP shared by every layer maps $\iota_{qj}$ to
a basis of kernel functions per pair, once per forward pass
(`_KernelBasis`), and each layer's kernel $\kappa_h$ is a learned
combination of them for each head $h$. With $\omega_j \equiv w_j / \sum_i
w_i$ the cell's share of the boundary measure, $\tilde h \equiv
\mathrm{LN}(h)$ (one LayerNorm for cells, one for points) and $c$ key
channels per head, the read after a layer is

$$
\alpha_{qjh} = \operatorname*{softmax}_j \Big( \kappa_h(\iota_{qj})
  + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{c}} \big\langle W^{\mathrm q}_h \tilde h_q,\ W^{\mathrm k}_h \tilde h_j \big\rangle
  + \log \omega_j \Big),
\qquad
h_q \leftarrow h_q + W^{\mathrm o} \Big[ \textstyle\sum_j \alpha_{qjh}\, W^{\mathrm v}_h \tilde h_j \Big]_{h} ,
$$

where the brackets concatenate the heads' value channels and $W^{\mathrm
o}$ starts at zero, so training begins from the model without the read.

```{python}
#| label: para-arch-read-constants
#| output: asis
import physicsnemo.experimental.models.isla.tree_read as TR
print(f"The read's constants are fixed in the class: {TR.KERNEL_READ_BASIS} kernel basis functions "
      f"(`KERNEL_READ_BASIS`), {TR.KERNEL_READ_HEADS} heads (`KERNEL_READ_HEADS`), $c = {TR.KERNEL_READ_KEY}$ key channels "
      f"per head (`KERNEL_READ_KEY`) and {TR.KERNEL_READ_WIDTH // TR.KERNEL_READ_HEADS} value channels per head "
      f"(`KERNEL_READ_WIDTH` ÷ `KERNEL_READ_HEADS`).")
```

The log measure fraction makes the read a quadrature
(@sec-isla-quadrature): with the kernel and key terms constant it is the
measure-weighted mean of the cells' values, and splitting a cell into two
coincident halves or rescaling every measure changes nothing
(`test_tree_read_similarity_refinement_and_measure_scale_at_theta_zero`).
Every input is an invariant, so the read keeps the contracts of
@sec-isla-contracts, and it leaves the boundary tokens and the slices
untouched, so it keeps query independence
(`test_tree_read_is_exactly_query_independent_at_every_theta`). Evaluated
pair by pair it costs $Q \times N$ pairs per layer: $4 \times 10^{10}$ for
200,000 points around a 200,000-cell car.

#### The read through a cluster forest {#sec-arch-tree-read}

**The read runs through a Barnes–Hut forest at the opening angle $\theta =
1$: a point reads nearby cells one by one and each distant cluster of
similarly oriented cells as one virtual cell, which keeps the prediction
exactly query-independent and pose-invariant; the frame the forest is
built in only groups cells for speed.** ISLA-DTT is ISLA with read-only prediction points, the global
read after every layer and the forest at $\theta = 1$, all set by
`query_independent=True`. The forest is built once per case, without
gradient (`BoundaryForest`):

1. The frame is the boundary's own canonical frame: centered on the cells'
   measure-weighted centroid, with the principal axes of their
   measure-weighted position covariance, each signed so that the third
   moment of the positions along it is positive (`canonical_frame`). The
   forest is built in these coordinates, so it moves with the body. This is
   the one place in the class where a center and axes are estimated, and
   they decide only which cells share a cluster. No learned map reads them,
   so a tie of the frame does not make the prediction jump by $O(1)$, as it
   does for a network fed canonical coordinates (@sec-landscape-symmetry).
2. The cells are split by the sign octant of their normal in that frame,
   and one cluster tree is built per octant
   (`physicsnemo.mesh.spatial.ClusterTree`, which bisects the boxes of a
   Morton space-filling curve down to leaves of `TREE_READ_LEAF_SIZE`
   cells). Opposite normals never share a tree, so no cluster spans both
   faces of a thin body.
3. Every node holds a virtual cell: its cells' measure-weighted centroid,
   their renormalized measure-weighted mean normal, their mean vector
   channels and their total measure, and at every layer the
   measure-weighted means of their keys and values. The means are sums over
   a tree of pairwise sums in the working precision, float64 in a float64
   model and float32 otherwise, bfloat16 rows included (`node_means`), so a
   float64 model reads its clusters in float64 throughout.
4. Each point walks every tree once. A node is read as one virtual cell
   when its box diagonal is below $\theta$ times the distance from the point
   to the box and its normals are coherent: their measure-weighted RMS chord
   about the mean, $\sqrt{2(1 - \lvert \bar n \rvert)}$, is below $\theta$. A
   leaf that fails either test is read cell by cell, and any other node
   hands the point to its two children, so every cell is read exactly once,
   alone or inside one virtual cell
   (`test_point_pairs_admit_only_separated_coherent_nodes_and_cover_every_cell`).

The softmax of the global read then runs over each point's list, a virtual
cell entering with its total measure fraction as its log bias and its
invariants computed from its centroid and normal. Because the read is a
quadrature, a virtual cell is its cluster's monopole: were the logit
constant over the cluster, reading the virtual cell would equal reading its
cells one by one. The softmax of each point runs in a fused Triton kernel
that keeps nothing per pair between the forward and backward passes
(`segment_softmax_read`).

Three properties hold by construction. At $\theta = 0$, a setting of the
tests, no cluster is admitted and the read is the read of every cell pair
by pair (`test_tree_read_at_theta_zero_is_the_exact_read`). At every
$\theta$ a point's list depends on the forest and the point alone, so the
prediction is query-independent. And a rotation, reflection or translation
of the case gives the same forest and the same lists
(`test_forest_and_every_list_are_the_same_in_every_pose_at_finite_theta`),
so ISLA-DTT is pose-invariant. The frame can tie: two equal principal
variances, or an axis without a third moment, whose sign then follows
whichever of the dataset's axes it overlaps most. There a rigid motion can regroup the
clusters, and the read moves only at the size of the tree's error, which
vanishes as $\theta \to 0$. $\theta$ is a constant of the class (`TREE_READ_THETA`), not
an argument: ISLA-DTT trains and is scored at $\theta = 1$, so its kernel,
keys and values are learned as the forest groups the cells. The tree's error
is also what moves ISLA-DTT under an exact refinement of the boundary: on
the AirfRANS interior task, with the pair trained with the compiled path
after its fault was fixed, splitting the airfoil's panels raises its
pressure error by `{python} f"{min(DTT_REFINE) - 1:.1%}"` to
`{python} f"{max(DTT_REFINE) - 1:.1%}"` at $\theta = 1$, and on an ISLA-DTT
pair trained under the compiled-path fault, read at $\theta = 0$, the same
refinements move its error by at most `{python} f"{DTT_THETA0:.1%}"`
(@sec-remesh-measured).

```{python}

ANC = RES / "campaigns_2026-10-18" / "anchor" / "readout"

for a, lab in ARMS:

    DA[a] = dict(rat=rat, below=below, dev=posed_dev(a), step=step(a) / step("isla"), peak=peak(a))
    out += (f"| {lab} | {' / '.join(f'{x:.5f}' for x in vals)} | {'–' if a == 'isla' else ' / '.join(f'{x:.3f}' for x in rat)} | "
            f"{'–' if a == 'isla' else (', '.join(below) or 'none')} | {100 * DA[a]['dev']:.2f}% | {DA[a]['step']:.2f} | {DA[a]['peak']:.1f} |\n")

      "seed of interacting ISLA; the posed column is the largest change of a seed's error under the rotated and translated "
      "scoring, over fields and seeds; step time is the median at epoch 250 on one GB300, and peak memory as the training "
      "log reports it (rank 0). Results: results/campaigns_2026-10-18/anchor/readout/scores.json and cost_partial.json; "
      "the registered rule and its outcome: results/campaigns_2026-10-18/anchor/RESULTS.md. How to read this: a ratio "
      "compares a design with interacting ISLA, below one meaning the design is more accurate; it is not a baseline "
      "comparison.")
```

## What the pass never does {#sec-arch-never}

**The contracts of @sec-isla-contracts are absences, and two of them can be
read off the stages directly.**

- **No coordinate reaches a learned map, and no center enters one.**
  ISLA-DTT's forest is built in a canonical frame of the boundary
  (@sec-arch-tree-read), which decides only which cells are grouped for
  speed, not what a learned map reads. $r_i$ enters only as $r_i - z_s$ (step d), $r_i - \sum_s \pi^f_{is} z^f_s$
  (stage 4), $x_q - p_q$ (the prediction points' geometry) and $r_q - r_j$
  (the boundary read). Every learned input is the constant 1, a norm, a dot
  product, a logarithm or soft logarithm of one of those, or a supplied
  scalar; no input names a token's condition. The one mean position
  computed, inside $L$, is consumed by a scalar. Anchors are means over *slices*, not over
  the body, and only their differences from tokens are used.
- **No positional encoding, and no prediction point attends to another.**
  Tokens exchange information through the $M$ slice states, and the routing
  that decides which slice a token joins is a function of the token's state
  and its relation to the anchors. The one pairwise read in the class is the
  global boundary read of ISLA-DTT (@sec-arch-global-read): a read-only
  prediction point attends to boundary cells, and nothing flows from it to
  any token.

## Where the time and memory go {#sec-arch-cost}

**A training step of ISLA is limited by how many bytes it moves between the
GPU's memory and its arithmetic units, not by how much arithmetic it does,
and the largest thing it could move is one tensor: the relational
invariants $\xi_{is}$, one row per token–slice pair.** This section gives
the three facts about a GPU that a numerical analyst needs to read that
sentence, then follows them through ISLA.

**Three facts about a GPU.** First, a GPU has two kinds of memory. The
large one, *HBM* (high-bandwidth memory), holds every tensor; it is
hundreds of gigabytes and sits off the compute die. The small one is the
on-chip SRAM of each streaming multiprocessor, its registers and shared
memory: many orders of magnitude smaller, but read and written at a far
higher rate. Arithmetic happens only on data in SRAM. Second, the time of a
*kernel*, one function the GPU runs over many threads, is the larger of its
arithmetic time and its memory time. The ratio of the two is the kernel's
*arithmetic intensity*: floating-point operations per byte moved to or
from HBM. A kernel whose intensity is below the machine's balance point
waits on memory, however few flops it has. A large matrix multiply reuses
every byte it loads many times and is compute-bound; an elementwise
operation (a subtraction, a norm, a dot product of 3-vectors) touches each
byte once and is memory-bound. Third, PyTorch runs one kernel per operation
by default, and each kernel reads its inputs from HBM and writes its output
back to HBM. A chain of ten elementwise operations is ten round trips, and
each kernel launch has a fixed cost on the host whatever its size.
*Kernel fusion* writes the chain as one kernel that keeps the intermediates
in registers, so the chain costs one read and one write.

**Two facts about training.** A training step is a forward pass and a
reverse-mode (adjoint) pass. The reverse pass needs the forward
intermediates, the *activations*, so PyTorch keeps every tensor that a
later gradient reads until the reverse pass has used it; the peak memory of
a step is mostly these saved activations, not the parameters. *Activation
recompute* (checkpointing) keeps only a region's inputs and runs the region
again inside the reverse pass, trading flops for memory, as checkpointing
schemes for adjoint solvers do. And the recipe trains under *bf16
autocast*: matrix multiplies and other listed operations run in bfloat16, a
16-bit format with float32's exponent range and a short mantissa, while
reductions and everything else stay in float32.

```{python}
#| label: para-arch-bf16
#| output: asis
e16, e32 = torch.finfo(torch.bfloat16).eps, torch.finfo(torch.float32).eps
print(f"The unit roundoff of bfloat16 is {e16 / 2:.1e} against float32's {e32 / 2:.1e} (`torch.finfo`). That is "
      "adequate for a learned map and too coarse for geometry: a separation $r_i - z_s$ of two nearby positions "
      "loses most of its digits. ISLA therefore keeps its geometry in float32 under autocast. Every contraction of "
      "geometric vectors is a broadcast multiply-and-sum rather than an `einsum` (which autocast would run in bfloat16; "
      "`ISLA._dots`, `_relational_invariants`), the prediction points' geometry, the boundary draw and the conditions' "
      "vector and tensor maps run with autocast disabled, and the softmax of the prototype attention is taken in float32. "
      "The learned maps run in bfloat16.")
```

**ISLA's case: the $N \times M$ tensors.** Steps b to h of every slice
layer work on the grid of all token–slice pairs. The routing logits, the
two routing softmaxes, the refinement and the read-back weights are
$N{\times}M$ matrices, and the relational invariants are $N{\times}M$ in
their own width, built from the separations $\rho_{is}$ ($N{\times}M{\times}3$)
and their norms and directions. @tbl-arch-cost-sizes computes what these
tensors would occupy in HBM if they were written out and kept for the
reverse pass, at the reference configuration.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-arch-cost-sizes
#| output: asis
N_, M_, d_ = 200_000, REF.n_slices, REF.blocks[0].norm_mlp.normalized_shape[0]
G_, L_ = REF.blocks[0].n_geo, len(REF.blocks)
GiB = 2 ** 30
items = [
    ("relational invariants $\\xi_{is}$, float32", "$N{\\times}M{\\times}" + f"{G_}$", N_ * M_ * G_ * 4),
    ("the same, rounded to bfloat16 for the refinement's linear map", "$N{\\times}M{\\times}" + f"{G_}$", N_ * M_ * G_ * 2),
    ("separations $\\rho_{is}$ and their directions, float32", "$2 \\times N{\\times}M{\\times}3$", 2 * N_ * M_ * 3 * 4),
    ("distances $\\lvert\\rho_{is}\\rvert$, float32", "$N{\\times}M$", N_ * M_ * 4),
    ("one $N{\\times}M$ matrix of logits or weights, float32", "$N{\\times}M$", N_ * M_ * 4),
    ("for scale: the token state $h_i$, float32", "$N{\\times}D$", N_ * d_ * 4),
    ("for scale: one MLP hidden activation, bfloat16", "$N{\\times}4D$", N_ * 4 * d_ * 2),
]
geo_stored = sum(b for (n, _, b) in items[:4])
out = "| tensor of one slice layer | shape | GiB per layer | GiB over the 12 layers |\n|---|---|--:|--:|\n"
for name, shape, b in items:
    out += f"| {name} | {shape} | {b / GiB:.2f} | {L_ * b / GiB:.1f} |\n"
out += f"| **the geometry region's intermediates (first four rows)** | | **{geo_stored / GiB:.1f}** | **{L_ * geo_stored / GiB:.0f}** |\n"
print(out)
print(f": Size of the per-layer tensors of ISLA in the reference configuration at $N$ = {N_:,} tokens, $M$ = {M_} slices, width "
      f"$D$ = {d_} and invariant width {G_} ($5 + K$ with $K = 1$), computed from the shapes as the page renders. How to read "
      "this: these are the bytes each tensor would hold if it were written to HBM and kept for the reverse pass; the eager "
      "path rebuilds the geometry rows in the reverse pass and the fused kernel never writes them, so neither stores them. "
       "The table does not show what a step actually allocates, which the measurements below give.")
```

```{python}
#| label: para-arch-cost-fit
#| output: asis
FRONT = json.load(open(RES / "char" / "ref80_frontier_2026-10-02.json"))["candidates"]["isla_w512_s512"]
print(f"Kept for the reverse pass, the geometry region alone would need {L_ * geo_stored / GiB:.0f} GiB over the twelve "
      f"layers. The whole training step of the reference configuration on the DrivAerML Surface task peaks at "
      f"{FRONT['train_peak_gib']:.0f} GiB per GPU (four GB300 ranks, bfloat16, the maximum over ranks; "
      "results/char/ref80_frontier_2026-10-02.json, measured with the raw-read variant, which has the same parameters and "
```

@fig-arch-intensity counts the arithmetic intensity of the main operations
of one slice layer from their shapes. The matrix multiplies of the learned
maps and of the slice pooling and read-back do hundreds of operations per
byte they move; the eager geometry on the token–slice grid does less than
one, so its time is the time to move its bytes. Fusing the geometry into one
kernel raises its intensity by more than an order of magnitude, and it is
still on the memory-bound side.

```{python}
#| label: fig-arch-intensity
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Arithmetic intensity of the main operations of one slice layer in the
#|   reference configuration ($N$ = 200,000 tokens, $M$ = 512 slices, width
#|   $D$ = 512, $K = 1$), counted from the shapes: floating-point operations
#|   divided by the bytes each operation reads from and writes to HBM, with
#|   bfloat16 operands for the matrix multiplies (blue) and float32 for the
#|   operations on the token–slice grid (violet). The eager geometry is
#|   counted operation by operation as PyTorch runs it; the fused kernel reads
#|   the logits once and writes the refinement, the read-back weights and the
#|   pooled invariants once. How to read this: further right is more
#|   arithmetic per byte; a GPU's balance point lies far to the right of every
#|   violet bar, so those operations are limited by memory traffic. This is a
#|   count, not a measurement: it ignores caches, the reverse pass and launch
#|   costs. Computed as the page renders.
#| code-fold: true
N, M, d, K = 200_000, REF.n_slices, REF.blocks[0].norm_mlp.normalized_shape[0], 1
G = 5 + K
mm = lambda m, k, n, b=2: (2 * m * k * n, b * (m * k + k * n + m * n))   # (flops, bytes) of an (m x k) @ (k x n)
ops = [
    ("token MLP, up-projection $N{\\times}D \\to N{\\times}4D$", *mm(N, d, 4 * d), BLUE),
    ("token MLP, down-projection", *mm(N, 4 * d, d), BLUE),
    ("broadcast $W_b$ on $[\\tilde h; b; \\gamma]$", *mm(N, 5 * d // 2, d), BLUE),
    ("routing logits against $M$ prototypes", *mm(N, d, M), BLUE),
    ("slice pooling $Z = a^{T} \\tilde h$", *mm(M, N, d), BLUE),
    ("read-back $b = \\pi Z$", *mm(N, M, d), BLUE),
]
# The eager geometry on the N x M grid, operation by operation (float32; per token-slice pair:
# floating-point operations, bytes read and written to HBM; the broadcast N- and M-sized operands are negligible).
per_pair = [
    (3, 12),            # rel = r - z: write 3 floats
    (5, 12 + 4),        # |rel|: read 3, write 1
    (1, 4 + 4),         # log |rel|
    (3, 12 + 4 + 12),   # rel_hat = rel / |rel|: read 3 + 1, write 3
] + [(5, 12 + 4)] * (K + 3) + [   # the K + 3 dot products: read 3, write 1
    (0, 2 * 4 * G),     # concatenate into xi: read and write G floats
    (2 * G, 4 * G + 4), # refinement w_g . xi + b_g: read G, write 1
    (5, 3 * 4 + 4),     # read-back softmax over slices of logits + bias
    (2 * G, 4 + 4 * G), # pooled invariants: read pi and xi
]
fl_e, by_e = sum(f for f, _ in per_pair), sum(b for _, b in per_pair)
ops += [
    ("softmax over points (one $N{\\times}M$ pass)", 5 * N * M, 8 * N * M, VIOLET),
    ("relational geometry, eager, operation by operation", fl_e * N * M, by_e * N * M, VIOLET),
    ("relational geometry, fused kernel", fl_e * N * M, 3 * 4 * N * M, VIOLET),
]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 3.9))
y = np.arange(len(ops))[::-1]
for yy, (name, fl, by, col) in zip(y, ops):
    I = fl / by
    ax.barh(yy, I, color=col, height=0.62)
    ax.text(I * 1.12, yy, f"{I:,.1f}" if I < 10 else f"{I:,.0f}", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
ax.set_yticks(y); ax.set_yticklabels([o[0] for o in ops], fontsize=8.8)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlim(0.1, 3000)
ax.set_xticks([0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000]); ax.set_xticklabels(["0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1,000"])
ax.set_xlabel("arithmetic intensity [floating-point operations per byte of HBM traffic]")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
for sp in ("top", "right"): ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

**The eager region is checkpointed.** Steps c to e and the pooling of step
h are one *geometry region* per layer (`_geo_region`): a function of
$(\lambda, r, \hat n, \hat g, z, m)$ whose only parameters are $w_g, b_g$,
returning the refinement $N{\times}M$, the read-back weights $N{\times}M$
and the pooled invariants $N{\times}(5+K)$. On the eager path the block
calls it under `torch.utils.checkpoint`, so the separations, distances and
invariants live only inside the region: the reverse pass rebuilds them from
the region's inputs, with outputs and gradients bitwise equal to storing
them. Pooling before projecting (step h) is what keeps the region's
output small: projecting every pair to width $D/2$ first would make the
saved tensor $N{\times}M{\times}D/2$ instead of $N{\times}(5+K)$.

**The fused kernel never writes them.** On CUDA, the model replaces the
region by two Triton kernels, one for the forward pass and one for the
reverse pass (`geo_kernel.py`). The forward
kernel loads a tile of tokens and all $M$ anchors into on-chip memory,
forms the separations, invariants, refinement and both softmax inputs in
registers, and writes only the refinement, the read-back weights and the
pooled invariants. The backward kernel rebuilds the invariants inside the
tile from the $N{\times}3$ and $M{\times}3$ geometry and writes the
gradient of the logits once. Per-slice reductions are written as per-tile
partial sums and reduced by PyTorch, so the result is deterministic. The
kernel rounds to bfloat16 exactly where autocast would, so its forward
equals the eager forward up to the order of floating-point summation. Even
`torch.compile`, which fuses the elementwise chain, still writes the
$N{\times}M{\times}(5+K)$ invariants (once in float32, once in bfloat16)
in the forward pass and again in the reverse pass; the region is
memory-bound, so its cost is that traffic.

```{python}
#| label: para-arch-cost-paths
#| output: asis
MR = json.load(open(RES / "isla_memory_recompute_2026-09-07.json"))["runs"]["20000"]
CS = {(r["arm"], r["tokens"]): r for r in json.load(open(RES / "cost_sweep_gb300_bf16_2026-09-18.json"))["runs"] if r.get("status") == "ok"}
_med = lambda v: float(np.median(v))
rc, fu = CS[("isla_compiled_recompute", 200000)], CS[("isla_fused_compiled", 200000)]
print(f"Two measurements on a smaller ISLA show the size of each effect. Recompute: at {MR['n_tokens']:,} tokens the step's "
      f"peak memory falls from {MR['peak_step_memory_gib']['stored']:.1f} GiB with the region's intermediates stored to "
      f"{MR['peak_step_memory_gib']['recompute']:.1f} GiB with them rebuilt, at {MR['step_ms']['recompute_over_stored_median']:.2f} "
      f"times the step time, with a bitwise-equal forward (results/isla_memory_recompute_2026-09-07.json, one RTX 4090). "
      f"Fusion: at 200,000 tokens the compiled model with the checkpointed eager region steps in {_med(rc['step_ms']):.0f} ms, "
      f"the same model with the fused kernel in {_med(fu['step_ms']):.0f} ms, {_med(rc['step_ms']) / _med(fu['step_ms']):.1f} "
      f"times faster, at {rc['peak_allocated_gib']:.1f} against {fu['peak_allocated_gib']:.1f} GiB "
      f"(results/cost_sweep_gb300_bf16_2026-09-18.json, one GB300, bfloat16). Instrument: ISLA at 192 wide, 12 layers, "
      f"256 slices, raw slice reads, random inputs (@sec-study-configurations); the costs are of the operations, which these "
      f"configurations share with the reference configuration up to width and slice count.")
```

**The softmax over points is taken after a transpose.** Steps b and f
normalize an $N{\times}M$ matrix over its *first* axis, the tokens. PyTorch
stores the matrix with the slice axis contiguous, and its softmax kernel for
a non-last axis parallelizes over the other axes and walks the reduced axis
serially, so a softmax over 200,000 tokens runs 200,000 dependent steps per
column. The class transposes, takes the softmax along the contiguous last
axis with the row-parallel kernel, and transposes back
(`_softmax_over_points`). Its docstring gives the measured effect:

```{python}
#| label: code-softmax-over-points
#| output: asis
listing("blocks.py", "_softmax_over_points", docstring=True)
```

**The whole model compiles to one graph.** `torch.compile` traces the
Python forward into a graph of tensor operations (TorchDynamo) and
generates fused GPU kernels for it (TorchInductor), which removes most of
the elementwise round trips and kernel launches outside the geometry
region. The recipe compiles ISLA whole, `Mesh` inputs and output included,
with `fullgraph=True` (no breaks in the trace) and `dynamic=True` (the token
counts are symbols, so one graph serves every mesh size and the case-to-case
change in cell count does not recompile). The fused geometry kernel is a
registered custom operator and stays a leaf of the graph. Some of the
class's code exists only to keep that graph single: the token count's
logarithm is computed as a tensor under compile, since `math.log` of a
symbolic size would fix it (`_log_count`), and a guard tells the compiler
that a flattened token axis divides by the token count (`_hint_token_axis`).
ISLA-DTT is the exception. Its forest and each point's list of sources are
sized by the data, which breaks a fullgraph trace, so it compiles each slice
block separately instead (`compile_blocks=True`, @sec-arch-switches). So
does ISLA on AeroZoo: on its four boundary meshes the compiler ties the
sizes of meshes whose cell counts are equal in the first case and guards
the input meshes' caches by their size, so the whole-model graph recompiles
case after case, and `isla_volume_aerozoo.yaml` compiles per block.

**Where a training step's time goes.** @fig-arch-step-breakdown takes one
warm training step of ISLA and of ISLA-DTT apart on AeroZoo, on one node of
four GB300 GPUs under data parallelism (each GPU trains on its own case and
the gradients are averaged across them, an *all-reduce*, during the reverse
pass). The profile is of the code of the nearest-token form
(@sec-checkpoint-form): the datapipe drew the boundary tokens, and the
prediction points' geometry came from a search for the nearest boundary
token. It does not time the in-model draw or the exact surface search of
@sec-arch-interior-geometry, and the book gives no measurement of those
two stages' cost.

```{python}
#| label: fig-arch-step-breakdown
#| fig-cap: >
#|   One warm training step of ISLA and of ISLA-DTT at their reference
#|   configurations on AeroZoo (`family_non_box` split, 200,000 interior
#|   cells, bfloat16, per-block compile, one node of four GB300 GPUs, data
#|   parallel; mean over 150 steps and the four ranks). (a) The wall time of
#|   the step by phase (upper bar of each pair), and the time the GPU spends
#|   running kernels in each phase (lower bar, from the profiler, collective
#|   communication excluded); the gap between the two bars is time the GPU
#|   waits. (b) The forward pass by module, synchronized at each module
#|   boundary. How to read this: the backward phase includes the wait for the
#|   gradient all-reduce, which is time the GPUs spend waiting for the
#|   slowest of them; the data phase is the main thread preparing the next
#|   case, measured with that preparation at the start of the step, where
#|   the recipe runs it during the reverse pass (see the text). The
#|   module "nearest-token geometry" is the nearest-token form's search
#|   (@sec-checkpoint-form), not the exact geometry. Data:
#|   results/perf_2026-10-18/step_breakdown.json.
#| code-fold: true
PB = json.load(open(RES / "perf_2026-10-18" / "step_breakdown.json"))
HT, GK, FM = PB["host_timeline_ms"], PB["gpu_kernels_ms"], PB["forward_modules_ms"]
PH = [("data", ("data_consume", "data_collective"), MUTED), ("forward", ("fwd_host", "fwd_collective"), VIOLET),
      ("backward and all-reduce wait", ("bwd_host", "gradnorm_drain"), "#b3abe0"), ("optimizer and logging", ("opt_host", "log"), BASELINE)]
GPH = {"data": ("data",), "forward": ("fwd",), "backward and all-reduce wait": ("bwd",), "optimizer and logging": ("opt",)}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 6.2), gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.95, height_ratios=[1.25, 1.0]))
ax = axes[0]
for row, (key, name) in enumerate((("isla", "ISLA"), ("isla_dtt", "ISLA-DTT"))):
    y0 = 1.6 * (1 - row)
    x = 0.0
    for lab, parts, col in PH:
        w = sum(HT[key][p] for p in parts)
        ax.barh(y0 + 0.32, w, left=x, height=0.5, color=col, edgecolor=WHITE)
        if w > 60:
            ax.text(x + w / 2, y0 + 0.32, f"{w:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8, color=WHITE if col == VIOLET else INK)
        x += w
    ax.text(x + 12, y0 + 0.32, f"step {HT[key]['step']:,.0f} ms", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
    x = 0.0
    for lab, parts, col in PH:
        w = sum(GK[key][p] for p in GPH[lab])
        ax.barh(y0 - 0.3, w, left=x, height=0.5, color=col, edgecolor=WHITE, alpha=0.85)
        x += w
    ax.text(x + 12, y0 - 0.3, f"GPU kernels {x:,.0f} ms", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=MUTED)
ax.set_yticks([1.6, 0.0]); ax.set_yticklabels(["ISLA", "ISLA-DTT"], fontsize=9.5)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1750); ax.set_xlabel("time per training step [ms]")
ax.set_title("(a) the step by phase: wall time (upper) and GPU kernel time (lower)", fontsize=9.5, loc="left")
ax.legend(handles=[plt.Rectangle((0, 0), 1, 1, color=c) for _, _, c in PH], labels=[l for l, _, _ in PH],
          fontsize=8, ncol=4, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.3), frameon=False)
for sp in ("top", "right"): ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax = axes[1]
MODS = [("slice blocks", lambda m: m["blocks"], VIOLET), ("nearest-token geometry", lambda m: m["nearest_boundary_geometry"], AQUA),
        ("tree: forest build", lambda m: m.get("tree_forest_build", 0), "#5f5e58"),
        ("tree: walk, plan and basis", lambda m: m.get("tree_walk", 0) + m.get("tree_pair_plan", 0) + m.get("tree_basis", 0), MUTED),
        ("tree reads", lambda m: m.get("tree_reads", 0), BASELINE)]
for row, (key, name) in enumerate((("isla", "ISLA"), ("isla_dtt", "ISLA-DTT"))):
    m = FM[key]; x = 0.0
    for lab, f, col in MODS:
        w = f(m)
        if w:
            ax.barh(1 - row, w, left=x, height=0.55, color=col, edgecolor=WHITE)
            if w > 45:
                ax.text(x + w / 2, 1 - row, f"{w:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8, color=WHITE if col in (VIOLET, "#5f5e58") else INK)
        x += w
    rest = m["total"] - x
    ax.barh(1 - row, rest, left=x, height=0.55, color=WHITE, edgecolor=MUTED, lw=0.6)
    ax.text(m["total"] + 10, 1 - row, f"forward {m['total']:.0f} ms", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
ax.set_yticks([1, 0]); ax.set_yticklabels(["ISLA", "ISLA-DTT"], fontsize=9.5)
ax.set_xlim(0, 750); ax.set_xlabel("time in the forward pass, synchronized [ms]")
ax.set_title("(b) the forward pass by module (open: the rest)", fontsize=9.5, loc="left")
ax.legend(handles=[plt.Rectangle((0, 0), 1, 1, color=c) for _, _, c in MODS], labels=[l for l, _, _ in MODS],
          fontsize=8, ncol=3, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.4), frameon=False)
for sp in ("top", "right"): ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: para-arch-step-breakdown
#| output: asis
gb = lambda k: PB["gpu_busy_unprofiled_fraction"][k]
pa = PB["prefetch_ab_ms"]
sav = sorted(100 * (1 - np.mean(r["fix"]) / r["base"]) for r in (pa["isla_aba_269723"], pa["isla_abab_270549"]))
ri, dd = PB["rank_imbalance"], PB["ddp_allreduce"]
bc, sy, mem = PB["boundary_cells_per_rank"]["isla"], PB["host_syncs_per_step"]["isla_dtt"], PB["peak_memory_gib"]
FMi, FMd = FM["isla"], FM["isla_dtt"]
print(f"**The step is bound by the GPU, and what is left is waiting.** ISLA's warm step takes {HT['isla']['step']:,.0f} ms and keeps "
      f"the GPUs running kernels for about {100 * gb('isla'):.0f}% of it; its forward and reverse passes issue their kernels faster "
      f"than the GPU runs them ({HT['isla']['fwd_host']:.0f} ms of host time against {GK['isla']['fwd']:.0f} ms of kernels in the "
      f"forward, {HT['isla']['bwd_host']:.0f} against {GK['isla']['bwd']:.0f} in the reverse pass). In the forward, the twelve slice "
      f"blocks take {FMi['blocks']:.0f} of {FMi['total']:.0f} ms and that form's nearest-token search of the prediction points "
      f"{FMi['nearest_boundary_geometry']:.0f}. The optimizer is a small share: Muon stacks the matrices of equal shape and orthogonalizes "
      f"them in one batched Newton–Schulz iteration, {HT['isla']['opt_host']:.0f} ms of host time per step. Two costs are real. The "
      f"first is rank imbalance: the datapipe of that form gave the four GPUs different numbers of boundary tokens ({bc['mean']:,} on "
      f"average, {bc['max']:,} on the fullest; the in-model draw keeps exactly $\\min(\\text{{cells}}, B)$, which this profile does "
      f"not measure), the forward of the slowest rank runs {ri['isla_fwd_max_minus_mean_ms'][0]} to {ri['isla_fwd_max_minus_mean_ms'][1]} ms "
      f"longer than the mean, and with the reverse pass the others wait {ri['isla_step_cost_ms'][0]} to {ri['isla_step_cost_ms'][1]} ms "
      f"per step ({100 * ri['isla_step_cost_fraction'][0]:.0f} to {100 * ri['isla_step_cost_fraction'][1]:.0f}%). The all-reduce kernels "
      f"take {dd['isla_bwd_nccl_kernel_ms'][0]} to {dd['isla_bwd_nccl_kernel_ms'][1]} ms of the reverse pass while moving the gradients "
      f"takes {dd['pure_transfer_ms']} ms: that time is waiting for the slowest rank, not bandwidth. The second is data preparation: "
      f"the main thread moves the next case to the GPU and runs its transforms ({HT['isla']['data_consume']:.0f} ms) in many small "
      f"kernels. Prepared at the start of a step, as in @fig-arch-step-breakdown, it runs while the GPU has just drained and sits "
      f"idle. The recipe loads the next batch right after the reverse pass is launched, while the GPU is still running it "
      f"(`_run_epoch` in `src/train.py`), with the same samples in the same order; against preparation at the start of the step, "
      f"that makes ISLA's step {sav[0]:.1f} to {sav[1]:.1f}% shorter on AeroZoo "
      f"({pa['isla_aba_269723']['base']} against {pa['isla_aba_269723']['fix']} ms, and {pa['isla_abab_270549']['base']} against "
      f"{np.mean(pa['isla_abab_270549']['fix']):.0f}, in two comparisons on one node). "
      f"Peak memory is {mem['isla']['allocated']} GiB allocated per GPU ({mem['isla']['reserved']} GiB reserved by PyTorch's caching allocator).")
print()
print(f"**ISLA-DTT's forward waits on the host.** Its step takes {HT['isla_dtt']['step']:,.0f} ms with the GPU busy about "
      f"{100 * gb('isla_dtt'):.0f}% of it, at {mem['isla_dtt']['allocated']} GiB allocated ({mem['isla_dtt']['reserved']} reserved). The Barnes–Hut forest is built from the data in each "
      f"forward ({FMd['tree_forest_build']:.0f} ms, of {FMd['tree_total']:.0f} ms for the whole tree stage), and its sizes are known "
      f"only on the host, so the forward synchronizes host and GPU {sy['fwd']} times per step and launches "
      f"{PB['kernel_launches_per_step']['isla_dtt']['fwd']:,} kernels against ISLA's {PB['kernel_launches_per_step']['isla']['fwd']:,}. "
      f"The slice blocks cost what they cost in ISLA ({FMd['blocks']:.0f} ms); the twelve tree reads add {FMd['tree_reads']:.0f}. "
      f"Its reverse pass is host-bound as well, which is why loading the next batch during it does not shorten its step. "
      "These are means over the warm steps of one profiled run of each model on one split. "
      "Data: results/perf_2026-10-18/step_breakdown.json.")
```

**How the step scales with the case.** On one GPU, from 100,000 tokens per case up, ISLA's memory grows linearly in
the number of tokens, as slice attention's $\mathcal{O}(NM)$ cost predicts, and so does its step time on the surface
task; on the volume task its step grows less than in proportion, from a fixed cost per step. @fig-cost-sweep measures both for every reference configuration, and
@tbl-cost-slopes gives what a token costs each of them.

## The switches {#sec-arch-switches}

**The class has one frame, one routing form, one length unit, one boundary
draw and one prediction-point geometry, and a short list of keyword-only
arguments: the three field declarations, the task, the role of the
prediction points, the boundary-token budget, the three sizes, one compile
knob, the spatial dimension, and the two dataset constants of the declared
scales.** @tbl-arch-switches
reads each default from the constructor's signature; the behavior that is
not an argument is described in the stages above.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-arch-switches
#| output: asis
WHAT = {
    "output_schema": ("5", "the output fields by name and rank spec (`{pressure: {rank: 0}, wss: {rank: 1}, stress: {rank: 2, symmetric: true}}`; `parity: odd` for a pseudotensor); each costs the coefficients of @tbl-arch-coeffs and is returned as a leaf of the output Mesh's `point_data` under its name. A dotted name (`surface.pressure`) is a nested leaf, in the output and in every input mapping. An output may declare `units` and a constant `scale` (@sec-using-scales)"),
    "boundary_schemas": ("1, 2, 3d", "the boundary conditions by name, each with the per-cell fields of rank 0 to 2 it alone carries (`{}` for a condition without fields, a field optionally with `units`, `scale` and `velocity_scale`, @sec-using-scales), stored sorted; `forward` takes any non-empty subset of the names, each condition's fields read from its own mesh's `cell_data`. Each condition has its own input layer (its column on the constant its learned offset) and its own vector and tensor maps onto the shared channels, whose contractions with $\\hat\\rho_{is}$ join the relational invariants (@sec-arch-frame, @sec-arch-seed)"),
    "global_schema": ("1, 2, 3d, 5", "per-case fields of rank 0 or 1, read from `global_data` by name: each rank-1 field is a global direction $\\hat g_k$ (one seed cosine, one relational cosine, two basis vectors); each rank-0 field widens the seed; a field may declare `units`, `scale`, `velocity_scale` or the `role` `density` or `viscosity` (@sec-using-scales)"),
    "reynolds": ("1, 2", "`{mean, std}`, the standardization of $\\log_{10}(U L / \\nu)$ over a split's training cases, appended to the global scalars as one column; required with a global of the role `viscosity` and refused without one; a dataset constant, which the recipe fills from the dataset file (@sec-using-scales)"),
    "output_stats": ("5", "`{name: {mean, std}}`, the dataset's constant standardization of each output after its units are restored, so the model returns the standardized targets the loss compares; a vector's mean is zero (@sec-using-scales)"),
    "interior": ("modes", "the task: `False` predicts at every boundary cell it is given and takes no prediction points; `True` draws its boundary tokens inside the model and predicts at the prediction points, which join the slice layers as tokens with their exact geometry against the full-resolution surface (@sec-arch-modes); implemented in two and three dimensions"),
    "query_independent": ("modes, after each layer", "interior task only: `True` is ISLA-DTT, with read-only prediction points (no routing mass) that read the boundary cells through the forest at $\\theta = 1$ after every slice layer (@sec-arch-passive-decoder); rank-2 boundary fields are refused with it"),
    "boundary_tokens": ("1, modes", "interior task only: the number of boundary tokens per case, drawn inside the model from the full-resolution boundary (the budget water-filled over the conditions, each cell drawn with probability proportional to its measure by a systematic draw along the Morton order, each kept cell carrying its Horvitz–Thompson measure; a random start in training, $u = 1/2$ in evaluation; @sec-arch-boundary-draw); a surface task reads every cell and accepts only the default"),
    "hidden": ("all", "the width $D$"),
    "n_layers": ("3", "the number of slice layers"),
    "n_slices": ("3, 4", "the slice count $M$ of every layer and of the head frame"),
    "compile_blocks": ("3", "run each slice block's forward under `torch.compile`, built lazily at the first call; parameter names, the state dict and the eager path are unchanged, and the fused geometry kernel stays a custom-op leaf. The way to compile ISLA-DTT, whose boundary read breaks the whole-model graph (@sec-arch-cost)"),
    "dim": ("all", "the spatial dimension: every boundary mesh is a `Mesh[dim - 1, dim]` (a polyline in two dimensions), every prediction point has `dim` coordinates, and the head's basis follows it (perpendiculars instead of cross products in two dimensions; odd-parity outputs refused for `dim >= 4`). A planar problem is passed with `dim=2`, never embedded with a zero third coordinate"),
}
sig = inspect.signature(ISLA.__init__).parameters
out = "| argument (default) | stage | what it sets |\n|:--------|:--|:----------------------------|\n"
for name in [n for n in sig if n != "self"]:
    dflt = sig[name].default
    dtxt = "required" if dflt is inspect.Parameter.empty else f"`{dflt!r}`"
    stage, what = WHAT[name]
    out += f"| `{name}` ({dtxt}) | {stage} | {what} |\n"
assert set(WHAT) == set(sig) - {"self"}
import physicsnemo.experimental.models.isla.geo_kernel as GK
out += (f"| `geo_kernel` attribute (`{REF.geo_kernel!r}`) | 3 | not an argument and not stored in a checkpoint: how the geometry region "
        f"runs, never what it computes. `\"auto\"` resolves at the first forward pass to the fused kernel when the inputs are on "
        f"CUDA, Triton is importable, `dim == 3`, there is at least one global direction, the global directions and the shared "
        f"vector channels number at most {GK.MAX_DIRECTIONS} together, there are at most {GK.MAX_SLICES:,} slices and no shared "
        f"tensor channel, and to the eager region otherwise (`resolve_geo_kernel`); set `\"eager\"` or `\"fused\"` to force one |\n")
print(out)
print(": The constructor's keyword-only arguments, each default read from `inspect.signature(ISLA.__init__)` as the page "
      "renders, and the one execution attribute. How to read this: `hidden`, `n_layers` and `n_slices` default to the reference "
      "configuration; `boundary_schemas` has no default, and every other default is the surface task with no global inputs.")
```
